extracted.intended_audience: academic peer reviewers (journal reviewers), researchers who write manuscript reviews
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing concise (1-2 page), constructive journal peer reviews that summarize claims, recommend decisions to editors, identify major and minor issues, and suggest feasible improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core principle: conscientious peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: "Peer review is broken. But let's do it as effectively and as conscientiously as possible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite systemic issues with peer review, reviewers should strive to conduct thorough, professional evaluations. Emphasize seriousness, fairness, and constructive engagement rather than cynicism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize manuscript and assess impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize the manuscript's main claims and assess its field impact
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin the review with a concise summary of the paper's main claims and a statement of its significance or expected impact in the field; this orients editors and authors to the reviewer's understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear decision recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct editors clearly—accept, reject, or revise recommendation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State an explicit recommendation (e.g., accept, reject, major/minor revision) so editors can quickly understand your overall judgment; back the decision with concise rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify major concerns with specific locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify major concerns with specific locations in the document
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List substantive, high-priority problems and cite exact locations (page, paragraph, figure, line) where the issue appears. Explain why each concern affects the paper's validity, claims, or suitability for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: List minor issues (grammar, references, clarity)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide lower-priority corrections (typos, reference errors, wording, formatting) separately from major concerns so authors can address them easily; marking them as optional helps prioritize work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how arguments could be strengthened through additional work
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how arguments could strengthen through additional analysis or experiments
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending additional analyses or experiments, be specific about what would strengthen the argument (e.g., particular controls, datasets, statistical tests) and how results would change interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep requested modifications reasonable in scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Stay reasonable in scope—avoid suggesting modifications requiring excessive time, cost, or resource commitment
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid asking for entirely new projects or prohibitively expensive experiments; if large work is essential, explain why and consider recommending rejection or major revision instead of minor edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard review structure and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard Structure (1-2 pages): Summary with significance assessment; Clear decision statement; Major concerns (if applicable); Minor concerns (optional)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a concise, well-structured review around 1–2 pages. Use clear headings (Summary, Recommendation, Major Concerns, Minor Concerns) for readability and to help editors and authors parse priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience orientation: editors primary, authors secondary
rubrics_metrics.description:
Primary audience: Journal editors need critical scientific feedback and claims evaluation

Secondary audience: Authors need suggestions for manuscript improvement
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame parts of the review for editors (e.g., overall recommendation and justification) and parts for authors (detailed, actionable comments). Remember reviewers are usually anonymous to authors but known to editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent document formatting
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent formatting conventions (headings, numbering, bulleting) across reviews to improve clarity. Clear formatting helps editors and authors quickly find and act on points raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide resolutions, not merely criticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite resolutions for major concerns (not just problems)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pointing out major flaws, propose specific ways to address them (analyses, experiments, re-interpretation) rather than only stating the problem. This makes the review more constructive and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend feasible, in-scope revisions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus suggestions on realistic changes the authors can implement within reasonable time and resource constraints. Distinguish between required experiments and optional enhancements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize comments by manuscript order with page references
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize comments by manuscript order with page references
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure detailed comments following the manuscript's order and include page/line references to help authors locate issues; this is especially helpful for copyediting and targeted rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain professional, diplomatic tone
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be respectful and constructive in language—critique the work, not the authors. Diplomacy increases the chance authors will engage with and accept suggested changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bias and disclose conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid bias and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from reviewing or tailor recommendations if you have a conflict of interest; disclose any potential conflicts to editors. Strive for impartial evaluation free from personal or professional bias.
